title: Help or Rescue

source.quote: whether by going along with something she doesn't want to do, by doing more than 50% of the work, or by not asking for what is wanted

setting: Sunday evening. Meher calls again - third time this year - about rent. Rahul picks up already half-knowing what's coming.

L1.line: I don't know what I'm going to do, I might actually lose the apartment this time. You're literally the only person who could help me right now.
L1.question: Is Meher asking Rahul for Help, or opening a Rescue?

options.text: Help - she's in real trouble and she's asking directly.
options.feedback: She's in real trouble, that part's true - but look again: has she actually asked for anything, or just described the crisis and named Rahul as the solution?

options.text: Rescue - there's no specific request yet, and "the only person who could help" puts the whole burden on Rahul before he's agreed to anything.
options.feedback: Right. Steiner's test isn't whether someone needs help, it's whether there's an actual request and the start of a two-sided contract - "you're the only one" is the Victim's opening move, not a request.

options.text: Can't tell yet - it depends on whether Rahul offers money or not.
options.feedback: Close, but the tell isn't what Rahul offers - it's whether anyone has named a specific ask yet. A Rescue can start before any money changes hands.

L1.lesson: Steiner's definition doesn't hinge on how real the crisis is - it hinges on whether there's a specific request and a two-sided contract. "You're the only one who can help" is a Rescue opener because it assigns Rahul the Rescuer role before he's agreed to anything or heard what's actually being asked.

L2.intro: Rahul wants to actually help Meher without quietly signing up to do more than half the work, again. What does he say?

beats.line: I don't know what I'm going to do, I might actually lose the apartment this time. You're literally the only person who could help me right now.
cues: framing Rahul as her only option

options.text: What exactly do you need, and what have you already figured out you can put toward it yourself?
options.outcome: A pause. "...Okay. I have maybe $300 saved. I need about $550 more." Specific, for the first time.
options.lesson: Naming the actual number and asking what she's already contributing turns a vague Rescue opener into something that can become a real contract - mutual consent needs a specific request from both sides, not just a crisis.

options.text: Of course, I'll transfer it to you right now, don't worry about it.
options.outcome: "Oh my god, thank you, you're a lifesaver." Relief - and the same call, same time, roughly the same amount, in about four months.
options.lesson: This is rule one and rule two of Rescue at once: doing something before you've thought about whether you actually want to, and doing 100% of the work. It feels generous tonight and costs the friendship slowly.

options.text: I can send you $150, but that's genuinely all I can do this time.
options.outcome: "Okay... I guess that helps some." She takes it, but nothing about what she'll do for the rest gets discussed.
options.lesson: The boundary is real and that matters, but handing over an amount without asking what she's contributing or planning still skips the contract - it's a smaller Rescue, not yet Help.

options.text: I can't keep bailing you out every few months, you need to actually deal with this.
options.outcome: Silence, then: "Wow. Okay. Forget it, I'll figure it out myself." She hangs up.
options.lesson: Refusing to Rescue is right in principle, but this lands as Persecution, not a boundary - Steiner's point is that Rescuer and Persecutor are the same unresolved resentment, just pointed in different directions.

fields.label: Draw the vectors for the full-Rescue reply and for the best reply.

pairs.label: "I'll transfer it right now, don't worry"

fields.label: In under 50 words: name Steiner's three tests for Rescue, and say which one Rahul's first instinct broke.

echo.setting: 72 hours later: Meher texts again, this time about her car.
echo.line: Can you just lend me $400? I'll pay you back, promise.
